name: NeurIPS Competitions Track
summary: The competition track running alongside the NeurIPS conference. Each year a set of independently organised competitions is selected on a wide range of problems — reinforcement learning, robustness, efficiency, scientific discovery — and the winners present at the conference. Formats vary a great deal between competitions, so read the individual rules rather than assuming a leaderboard.
requirements: Open to individuals and teams; registration is per competition. Most require a reproducible submission and, for the winning entries, a short report and presentation at the conference.
skillsPracticed: Problem framing under a fixed evaluation protocol, ablation discipline, and writing up results so an expert audience can reproduce them.
location: Conference host city; many competitions are run entirely online.

name: International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML)
summary: One of the three top-tier general machine learning venues, alongside NeurIPS and ICLR. ICML publishes across learning theory, optimization, deep learning, reinforcement learning and applications, and runs workshops and tutorials in the days around the main track.
requirements: Peer-reviewed submissions with a fixed page limit and a double-blind review period. Attendance requires registration; the conference runs annually, usually in July.
skillsPracticed: Reading a method section critically, identifying what is derived versus reported, and following the ablations that support a claim.

name: International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR)
summary: The major venue focused on representation learning, notable for running its review process publicly: submissions, reviews and author responses are open, and rejected papers remain readable with their reviews attached. That transparency makes it an unusually good place to learn how experts evaluate a paper.
requirements: Double-blind submission followed by an open review and rebuttal period. Attendance requires registration; the conference runs annually, usually in April or May.
skillsPracticed: Reading reviews as well as papers: what a strong rebuttal addresses, and which criticisms authors cannot answer.

name: CVPR Workshops and Challenges
summary: CVPR hosts dozens of workshops each year, many with an associated benchmark challenge on a specific vision problem — detection, segmentation, 3D reconstruction, video understanding. Challenges are evaluated on held-out test sets with a fixed protocol, which makes them one of the more trustworthy comparisons in the field.
requirements: Registration with the specific workshop challenge; submissions are usually capped per team and evaluated on a private test split.
skillsPracticed: Working against a fixed evaluation protocol you cannot tune, and engineering inference within submission limits.
location: Conference host city; challenge submissions are online

name: Kaggle Competitions
summary: The largest running set of data-science competitions, ranging from teaching-oriented playground events to research-grade featured competitions with prize pools. Leaderboards are split into public and private halves, and the private split is revealed only at the end — a deliberate defence against overfitting the visible score.
requirements: A free Kaggle account and acceptance of each competition's rules. Team merging is allowed up to a stated deadline; winning entries typically require a written solution.
skillsPracticed: Feature engineering, cross-validation design that matches the private split, and ensembling — plus the discipline of not overfitting a public leaderboard.

name: AIcrowd Challenges
summary: A platform hosting research-oriented challenges, frequently in reinforcement learning and multi-agent settings, several of which are attached to conferences such as NeurIPS. Many require an agent that runs inside a provided environment rather than a static prediction file, which makes them closer to real deployment than tabular competitions.
requirements: An AIcrowd account; each challenge specifies its environment, submission format and compute budget.
skillsPracticed: Reinforcement learning under an evaluation harness you do not control, reproducibility, and staying inside a stated compute budget.

name: DrivenData Competitions
summary: Competitions run with social-impact organisations on real problems — disaster response, public health, water infrastructure, climate. Datasets are genuinely messy and the metric is chosen by the partner organisation rather than by convenience, which is good preparation for applied work.
requirements: A free DrivenData account and agreement to the data-use terms set by the partner organisation.
skillsPracticed: Working with incomplete, biased and label-scarce data, and choosing a metric that matches an operational decision rather than a statistical convenience.

name: RoboCup
summary: An annual international robot soccer competition spanning several leagues — simulated 2D and 3D, humanoid, small and medium size, and rescue robotics. It is one of the longest-running embodied-AI benchmarks and forces perception, planning and control to work together under real time pressure.
requirements: Team registration well in advance, league-specific hardware or simulator compliance, and qualification in some leagues.
skillsPracticed: State estimation, multi-agent coordination, real-time control, and debugging a system where the environment is not reproducible.

name: International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence (IJCAI)
summary: The oldest major AI conference, running since 1969, with a broader scope than the machine-learning venues: planning, knowledge representation, reasoning under uncertainty, multi-agent systems and search sit alongside learning.
requirements: Peer-reviewed double-blind submission. The conference runs annually, usually in August, and proceedings are open access.
skillsPracticed: Reading symbolic and neurosymbolic work on its own terms rather than translating everything into a learning framework.

name: AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence
organizer: Association for the Advancement of Artificial Intelligence
summary: A broad annual AI conference covering learning, reasoning, planning, natural language processing, robotics, and AI ethics and safety. AAAI also runs a student abstract track and a case-study track on deployed applications, both useful for seeing work that is not purely benchmark-driven.
requirements: Peer-reviewed submission; the main track is double-blind. Held annually, usually in January or February.
skillsPracticed: Comparing how the same claim is argued in a learning paper versus a reasoning paper.
location: Rotating host city, frequently North America

name: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (ACL)
summary: The flagship natural language processing venue, together with its sibling meetings EMNLP and NAACL. ACL runs a reproducibility checklist for submissions and maintains the ACL Anthology, an open archive of the field's literature — the fastest way to trace the lineage of any NLP method.
requirements: Peer-reviewed submission with a completed reproducibility checklist. The meeting runs annually, usually in July.
skillsPracticed: Following a method's citation lineage, and checking whether an NLP result survives a change of tokenizer, dataset split or decoding setting.
